questions.question: What does it mean for $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ to be i.i.d.?
options: They have the same expectation and the same variance.
They are mutually independent but have different distributions.
They take exactly the same value in every outcome.
They are mutually independent and have the same distribution.

questions.question: What is guaranteed when two random variables are identically distributed?
options: Their probabilities agree for every interval of values.
Their possible values must be just zero and one.
They are independent.
They are equal in every outcome.

questions.question: Two separate independent tosses of the same coin have head indicators $X_1,X_2$ and head probability $p$. Which description fits?
options: Identically distributed but necessarily dependent.
Independent with necessarily different distributions.
I.i.d. Bernoulli variables with parameter $p$.
Equal indicators for every outcome.

questions.question: The head indicator $H$ and tail indicator $L$ from one fair toss are related by $L=1-H$. Which description is correct?
options: Dependent with the same distribution.
Independent with different distributions.
Independent with the same distribution.
Dependent with different distributions.

questions.question: Independent variables $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/3)$ and $Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(2/3)$ are best described how?
options: Equal to one another with probability one.
I.i.d. with parameter one half.
Identically distributed but not independent.
Independent but not identically distributed.

questions.question: Let $X$ be a fair Bernoulli variable and let $Y=X$. Which conclusion is valid?
options: The variables have different distributions.
They are identically distributed but not independent.
They are i.i.d. because their values agree.
They are independent because both means are one half.

questions.question: If $X_1,X_2$ are i.i.d. Bernoulli variables with $p=1/3$, what is $P(X_1=1,X_2=0)$?
For three i.i.d. Bernoulli variables with $p=1/2$, what is $P(X_1=1,X_2=0,X_3=1)$?
If $X_1,X_2$ are i.i.d. Bernoulli variables with $p=1/2$, what is $P(X_1=X_2)$?
Two variables have the same finite expectation. Which statement about identical distributions is correct?
options: They must have the same distribution.
They must have different distributions.
They must be mutually independent.
Equality of means is insufficient.

questions.question: Variables $X,Y$ satisfy $P(X=0)=P(X=1)=1/2$ and $P(Y=-1)=P(Y=2)=1/2$. What can be said about their marginals?
options: They are equal because both have two values.
They differ despite having the same mean.
They are equal because both have mean one half.
They are equal because both probabilities are one half.

questions.question: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_5$ be i.i.d. Which statement about the subcollection $X_2,X_4$ is guaranteed?
options: It is also i.i.d.
It is dependent because indices are skipped.
It is independent only when the variables are Bernoulli.
It has different marginal distributions.

questions.question: If $X_1,X_2$ are i.i.d. and $Y_i=2X_i+1$ for $i=1,2$, which conclusion holds?
options: The variables $Y_1,Y_2$ must equal $X_1,X_2$.
The variables $Y_1,Y_2$ necessarily become dependent.
The variables $Y_1,Y_2$ are i.i.d.
The variables $Y_1,Y_2$ necessarily have different distributions.

questions.question: Independent $X_1,X_2\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ are transformed to $Y_1=X_1$ and $Y_2=2X_2$. Which statement holds?
options: They remain independent but their distributions differ.
They become equal in every outcome.
They remain i.i.d. Bernoulli variables.
They become dependent, but with identical distributions.

questions.question: Two fair Bernoulli marginals have joint masses $P(0,0)=P(1,1)=0.4$ and $P(0,1)=P(1,0)=0.1$. Which conclusion is valid?
options: They are always equal to each other.
They have the same distribution but are dependent.
They are independent but have different marginals.
They are i.i.d. fair Bernoulli variables.

questions.question: Two variables have joint masses $P(0,0)=P(1,1)=0.1$ and $P(0,1)=P(1,0)=0.4$. Which conclusion is valid?
options: They are i.i.d. fair Bernoulli variables.
They are always opposite to each other.
They are identically distributed but dependent.
They have different Bernoulli parameters.

questions.question: Let $U,V$ be independent fair Bernoulli variables, and let $W=1$ when $U\ne V$ and zero otherwise. Are $U,V,W$ i.i.d.?
options: No: they share marginals but are not mutually independent.
Yes: every pair being independent is sufficient.
Yes: equal marginals alone establish i.i.d.
No: W has a different marginal distribution.

questions.question: All $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ equal the fixed constant $5$ in every outcome. Which statement is correct?
options: They fail to be random variables because they are constant.
Identical distributions, but necessarily dependent.
Independent variables, but necessarily different distributions.
They are i.i.d. with a degenerate distribution.

questions.question: Two independent variables each take values $0,1,2$ with probabilities $1/4,1/2,1/4$. What is $P(X_1+X_2=2)$?
For i.i.d. $X_1,X_2$ with common distribution function $F(t)=P(X_i\le t)$, which expression equals $P(X_1\le a,X_2\le b)$ for all real $a,b$?
options: $F(\min(a,b))$
$F(a)F(b)$
$F(a)F(a)$
